text: For the choir director. To the tune of "Do Not Destroy." A miktam of David.
Do you rulers really speak justice? Do you judge people with fairness?<f>The Hebrew word rendered "rulers" is uncertain; it may also mean "gods" (mighty ones) or "in silence."</f>

versions.text: Do you rulers really speak justice? Do you judge people with fairness?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'elem is textually difficult and has been understood as "silence," "gods/mighty ones," or (by revocalization) "rulers." A brief footnote would alert the reader that the interpretive choice is not the only possible reading, without disturbing the smooth oral rendering.

text: No—in your hearts you plot injustice, and your hands deal out violence in the land.
The wicked go astray from the womb; from birth they wander, speaking lies.
Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a deaf cobra that stops up its ear,
that will not listen to the voice of the charmers, however skilled the enchanter may be.
O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD!

versions.text: O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the lions, O LORD!
versions.explanation: Hebrew kephirim specifically denotes young lions in their prime and predatory strength, a nuance lost in the generic "lions." "Young lions" is also more vivid for oral reading and matches the imagery of aggressive attackers.

text: Let them vanish like water that drains away; when they aim their arrows, let them fall blunted.
Let them be like a slug that dissolves as it moves, like a stillborn child that never sees the sun.
Before your pots can feel the burning thorns, God will sweep the wicked away, green wood and blazing alike.

versions.text: Before your pots can feel the heat of the thorns—green or blazing—he will sweep them away.
versions.explanation: In the current wording the dashes and the pronouns "them" and "he" leave the subject and object unclear when read aloud; the reader cannot tell who is sweeping whom. Naming God as the subject and the wicked as the object preserves the sense of the Hebrew while making the line intelligible in oral reading.

text: The righteous will rejoice when they see vengeance done; they will bathe their feet in the blood of the wicked.
Then people will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on the earth."
